abstract: |
  This article sets out the notation of a linear structural equation model with
  a mean structure and describes model-implied instrumental-variable
  two-stage least squares (MIIV-2SLS) and the scaling and aggregated
  James–Stein estimators as implemented in lavaan. Both obtain factor
  loadings and latent regression slopes equation by equation without
  iterative optimization. The remaining variance and covariance parameters
  are subsequently estimated by reweighted least squares. For both
  procedures we state the estimators of the factor loadings and latent
  regression slopes, the subsequent estimation of the variance, covariance,
  and mean structure parameters, and the default covariance estimators of
  the factor loadings and latent regression slopes. For the
  James–Stein estimators we write the complete estimation procedure as a map
  from the sample moments to the parameter estimates and give the resulting
  delta method standard errors.

Structural equation models (SEMs) with latent variables are usually estimated
by maximum likelihood (ML), which estimates all parameters jointly. Despite
its desirable properties when its assumptions hold, ML has limitations that
can arise in practice. For instance, a misspecification in one equation can
bias estimates in other equations [@kaplan_1988; @bollen_etall_2007;
@bollen_2018; @dhaene_rosseel_2023; see also @jin_etall_2021, for diagonally
weighted least squares], and the iterative optimization can fail to converge
or end in inadmissible solutions, especially in small samples [@bollen_2018;
@dhaene_rosseel_2023]. Equation-by-equation estimators offer an alternative
[e.g., @bollen_1996; @burghgraeve_etall_2021]. In the approaches considered,
factor loadings and latent regression slopes are estimated one equation at a
time and in closed form, which may limit the propagation of misspecification
across equations and avoids iterative optimization for this part of the
estimation. Two such estimators are considered. Model-implied
instrumental-variable (MIIV) estimation replaces each latent variable by a
scaling indicator and uses instruments implied by the model to correct for the
resulting measurement error [@bollen_1996; @bollen_bauer_2004; @bollen_2018].
James–Stein estimation, proposed for SEMs by @burghgraeve_etall_2021, instead
replaces each latent predictor by an estimate of its conditional expectation
given observed proxies and then applies least squares. This conditional
expectation is estimated using James–Stein type shrinkage [@james_stein_1961;
@efron_morris_1973; @efron_morris_1975]. The approach follows the principle of
regression calibration in errors-in-variables regression [@fuller_1987;
@whittemore_1989; @carroll_etall_2006]. Moreover, its aggregated version uses
reliability weighted sums of indicators as proxies and was found to outperform
ML and MIIV in terms of mean squared error under the small sample conditions
examined [@burghgraeve_etall_2021]. Both versions were further evaluated for
confirmatory factor models by @dhaene_rosseel_2024.

Beyond point estimation, the usefulness of these approaches for statistical
inference depends on the accuracy of their standard errors. For MIIV,
conventional standard errors for factor loadings and latent regression slopes
follow from two-stage least squares [@bollen_1996]. For variance and
covariance parameters estimated subsequently by unweighted least squares,
standard errors accounting for the previously estimated loadings and latent
regression slopes were derived by @bollen_maydeuolivares_2007 and generalized
to other weight matrices by @jin_etall_2021. These calculations require derivatives of the estimated loadings and
latent regression slopes with respect to the sample moments, for which
@fisher_bollen_2020 provided explicit analytical expressions. More recently, @maydeuolivares_etall_2026 compared
subsequent variance and covariance estimation procedures and the accuracy of
their standard errors. For James–Stein estimation, @burghgraeve_etall_2021
derived a variance expression for latent regression estimates that accounts
for the estimated reliability adjustment. However, their empirical evaluations
used bootstrap standard errors for both the scaling and aggregated estimators,
and they did not provide a complete analytical standard error calculation
covering all estimation stages. Both approaches are now implemented in the R
package lavaan [@rosseel_2012], where analytical standard errors for the
scaling and aggregated James–Stein estimators are obtained by applying the
delta method to the complete estimation procedure [@lavaan_estimator_iv;
@lavaan_estimator_js].

## Present Study and Contributions

This article makes three minor contributions. First, it describes and
conceptually compares MIIV and James–Stein estimation within a common
notation, following their implementation in lavaan. Second, it develops and
illustrates a complete delta method calculation of standard errors for the
scaling and aggregated James–Stein estimators, accounting for uncertainty
across all estimation stages. Third, it evaluates their standard error
accuracy in a simulation study comparing both James–Stein estimators with MIIV
and ML.

The remainder of the article introduces the model and notation, describes the
estimation of factor loadings, latent regression slopes, and the remaining
parameters, presents the analytical standard errors, and reports the
simulation study.

# Model, Notation, and Parameterization

Following the all-y LISREL
notation [@joreskog_sorbom_1996, submodel 3B, Chapter 6; @rosseel_vidal_2025],
let $\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ contain the continuous observed variables and
$\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathbb{R}^q$ the latent variables. The measurement and latent variable models are

$$
\mathbf{y}
=
\boldsymbol{\nu}+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\eta}
+\boldsymbol{\epsilon},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\eta}
=
\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\eta}
+\boldsymbol{\zeta},
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ contains the measurement intercepts,
$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}$ contains the factor loadings,
$\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^q$ contains the structural intercepts,
and $\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q}$ contains the latent regression
slopes, that is, the regression slopes among the latent variables. The measurement errors
$\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ and structural disturbances
$\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in\mathbb{R}^q$ have zero means. 
Let $\mathbb{S}_+^k$ and $\mathbb{S}_{++}^k$ denote the sets of symmetric
positive semidefinite and positive definite $k\times k$ matrices,
respectively. Assume
$\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\boldsymbol{\Theta}\in\mathbb{S}_+^p$,
$\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\boldsymbol{\Psi}\in\mathbb{S}_+^q$,
and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\mathbf{0}_{p\times q}$.

Provided that $\mathbf{I}_q-\mathbf{B}$ is nonsingular, the latent and
observed mean vectors are

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_\eta
=
(\mathbf{I}_q-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\alpha}
\in\mathbb{R}^q,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\mu}_y
=
\boldsymbol{\nu}+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\mu}_\eta
\in\mathbb{R}^p,
$$
where $\mathbf{I}_q$ is the $q\times q$ identity matrix. The implied
observed covariance matrix is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
=
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\mathbf{I}_q-\mathbf{B})^{-1}
\boldsymbol{\Psi}
(\mathbf{I}_q-\mathbf{B})^{-\top}
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\top}
+
\boldsymbol{\Theta}.
$$

Both estimation procedures considered here require a scaling (marker)
indicator parameterization [@bollen_1996; @bollen_2018;
@burghgraeve_etall_2021], in which one loading per factor is fixed to one
and the corresponding measurement intercept is fixed to zero
[@bollen_1989]. Hence, let
$\mathbf{m}\in\mathbb{R}^q$ collect the scaling indicators from
$\mathbf{y}$, ordered so that the $k$-th element is the scaling indicator of
$\eta_{k}$ and loads on $\eta_{k}$ only, and let
$\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(m)}\in\mathbb{R}^q$ collect the corresponding
measurement errors. Then
$\mathbf{m}=\boldsymbol{\eta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(m)}$ and
$E(\mathbf{m})=\boldsymbol{\mu}_\eta$.

Let $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ collect the free
parameters, where $\mathcal{T}$ incorporates identification restrictions. Assume that
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^p$. Denote the
sample mean vector and covariance matrix by
$\overline{\mathbf{y}}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ and $\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{S}_+^p$,
respectively, computed from a single group of independent and identically
distributed observations $\mathbf{y}_i$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, of $\mathbf{y}$,
which is the setting of all estimation expressions below.^[Following
lavaan, $\mathbf{S}$ uses the divisor $n$ for the James–Stein estimators
and $n-1$ for MIIV estimation.] Define

$$
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\overline{\mathbf{y}}\\
\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf{S})
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^h,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\mu}_y(\boldsymbol{\theta})\\
\operatorname{vech}\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\}
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^h,
\qquad
h=p+\frac{p(p+1)}{2},
$$
where $\operatorname{vech}$ stacks the lower triangular entries, including
the diagonal.

# Estimation of Factor Loadings and Latent Regression Slopes

Model-implied instrumental-variable estimation and James–Stein estimation
obtain factor loadings and latent regression slopes equation by
equation [@bollen_1996; @bollen_2018; @burghgraeve_etall_2021]. Both
are estimated from centered observations, with intercepts estimated
subsequently. The following expressions assume that the loadings and latent
regression slopes being estimated are free and not subject to
equality constraints.

## Model-Implied Instrumental-Variable Estimation

In model-implied instrumental-variable (MIIV) estimation [@bollen_1996;
@bollen_2018], the scaling indicator equations are rearranged as

$$
\boldsymbol{\eta}_i
=
\mathbf{m}_i-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i^{(m)}
$$
and substituted into the remaining measurement and latent variable
equations. This latent to observed variable (L2O) transformation produces
equations involving observed dependent and explanatory variables, with
composite errors containing the original errors or disturbances and scaling
indicator measurement errors. The intercepts, factor loadings, and latent
regression slopes remain unchanged.

After centering and stacking observations, the $j$-th L2O equation has the
representation

$$
\mathbf{d}_j
=
\mathbf{X}_j\mathbf{a}_j+\mathbf{u}_j,
$$
where $\mathbf{d}_j\in\mathbb{R}^n$ contains the centered dependent
variable, which is an indicator in a measurement equation or the dependent
factor's scaling indicator in a latent variable equation. The matrix
$\mathbf{X}_j\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_j}$ contains the centered scaling
indicators of the $k_j$ latent predictors, $\mathbf{a}_j\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$
contains the corresponding loadings or latent regression slopes, and
$\mathbf{u}_j\in\mathbb{R}^n$ contains the composite errors. The
explanatory variables in $\mathbf{X}_j$ generally correlate with
$\mathbf{u}_j$ through their shared scaling indicator measurement errors.

The hypothesized model identifies observed variables that are uncorrelated
with the composite error and sufficiently related to the explanatory
variables. Let
$\mathbf{Z}_j\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times\ell_j}$ contain these centered
instruments, with $\ell_j\geq k_j$. In the first stage, the explanatory
variables are regressed on the instruments, giving

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_j
=
\mathbf{P}_j\mathbf{X}_j
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_j},
\qquad
\mathbf{P}_j
=
\mathbf{Z}_j
(\mathbf{Z}_j^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_j)^{-1}
\mathbf{Z}_j^{\top}
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.
$$

In the second stage, the dependent variable is regressed on these fitted
explanatory variables. The resulting MIIV two-stage least squares
(MIIV-2SLS) estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{j,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
(\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_j^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_j)^{-1}
\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_j^{\top}\mathbf{d}_j
=
(\mathbf{X}_j^{\top}\mathbf{P}_j\mathbf{X}_j)^{-1}
\mathbf{X}_j^{\top}\mathbf{P}_j\mathbf{d}_j,
$$
assuming that $\mathbf{Z}_j$ has full column rank and that
$\mathbf{Z}_j^{\top}\mathbf{X}_j$ has rank $k_j$.

## Scaling James–Stein Estimation

The James–Stein approach replaces the latent predictors in each equation by
estimates of their conditional expectations given observed proxies, followed
by least squares [@burghgraeve_etall_2021]. The implementation considered
here is restricted to recursive latent variable models without higher order
factors. Let $\mathcal{P}_j$ index the
$k_j$ latent predictors of equation $j$. The proxies are indicators that load
only on the corresponding latent predictor, with measurement errors
$\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(p)}_{j}$ such that
$\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(p)}_{j})$ is diagonal and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(p)}_{j},\epsilon_{d_j})=\mathbf{0}$,
where $\epsilon_{d_j}$ is the measurement error of the dependent variable.
For the latent variable equation of $\eta_k$, additionally
$\operatorname{Cov}(\zeta_k,\boldsymbol{\eta}_{\mathcal{P}_j})=\mathbf{0}$.
In the scaling version, the proxies are the scaling indicators, whose
equations are

$$
\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
=
\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
+
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(m)}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j},
$$
where all three vectors belong to $\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$. Define

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{mm,j}
=
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j})
\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{k_j},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j
=
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(m)}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j})
\in\mathbb{S}_+^{k_j}.
$$

Under joint normality,

$$
E(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}\mid\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j})
=
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}
+
\mathbf{R}_j
\left(
\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
-
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}
\right),
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$ and
$\mathbf{R}_j=(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{mm,j}-\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{mm,j}^{-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j\times k_j}$.

Note that, without normality, the same expression gives the best linear 
predictor under the stated covariance assumptions [@burghgraeve_etall_2021]. 
Preliminary measurement error variances are obtained using a Spearman type
procedure [@burghgraeve_etall_2021; @lavaan_estimator_js]. For indicator
$e$ with sample variance $s_{ee}$, the preliminary error variance is
$s_{ee}(1-\widehat{h}_e^{2})$, where the communality $\widehat{h}_e^{2}$
averages $s_{ef}s_{ef'}/(s_{ff'}s_{ee})$ over all pairs $(f,f')$ of other
indicators of the same latent variable. Incorporating the small sample
correction gives

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_j
=
\left(
\mathbf{S}_{mm,j}
-
c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j
\right)
\mathbf{S}_{mm,j}^{-1},
\qquad
c_n=\frac{n-3}{n-1},
$$
where $n>3$, $\mathbf{S}_{mm,j}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{k_j}$ is the sample
covariance matrix of the scaling indicators, and
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j\in\mathbb{S}_+^{k_j}$ is the diagonal
matrix of their preliminary measurement error variance estimates. These
preliminary error variance estimates are used for prediction and need not
equal the final model estimates.

Using the scaling indicator sample means
$\overline{\mathbf{m}}_{\mathcal{P}_j}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$, the fitted latent
predictors are

$$
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
=
\overline{\mathbf{m}}_{\mathcal{P}_j}
+
\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_j
\left(
\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
-
\overline{\mathbf{m}}_{\mathcal{P}_j}
\right)
\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}.
$$

Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_j\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_j}$ contain the centered
fitted predictors. Using the same dependent variable $\mathbf{d}_j$ as above,
the scaling James–Stein (JS) estimator of the loadings or latent
regression slopes in equation $j$ is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{j,\mathrm{JS}}
=
(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_j^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_j)^{-1}
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_j^{\top}\mathbf{d}_j.
$$

## Aggregated James–Stein Estimation

The aggregated James–Stein (JSA) estimator replaces each scaling indicator with a
weighted aggregate of indicators satisfying the proxy conditions above. For
latent predictor $\eta_k$ in equation $j$, let
$\mathbf{y}_{i,kj}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{kj}}$ collect these indicators, excluding
the dependent variable when estimating a measurement equation. Let
$\boldsymbol{\nu}_{kj}$, $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{kj}$, and $\mathbf{w}_{kj}$,
all in $\mathbb{R}^{r_{kj}}$, contain their intercepts, loadings, and
weights. Normalizing the aggregate to the latent variable's scale gives

$$
g_{ikj}
=
\frac{
\mathbf{w}_{kj}^{\top}
(\mathbf{y}_{i,kj}-\boldsymbol{\nu}_{kj})
}{
\mathbf{w}_{kj}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{kj}
}
=
\eta_{ik}+\epsilon^{(A)}_{ikj},
\qquad
\mathbf{w}_{kj}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{kj}\neq0.
$$

The weights are chosen to maximize reliability [@bentler_1968]. In the
sample,

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}
\in
\arg\max_{\mathbf{w}\neq\mathbf{0}}
\left\{
1-
\frac{
\mathbf{w}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kj}\mathbf{w}
}{
\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{S}_{kj}\mathbf{w}
}
\right\},
$$
where $\mathbf{S}_{kj}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{r_{kj}}$ is the sample covariance
matrix of the indicators in the aggregate and
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kj}\in\mathbb{S}_+^{r_{kj}}$
is the diagonal matrix of their preliminary measurement error variance
estimates. Preliminary loading estimates
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kj}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{kj}}$
from the scaling James–Stein estimator supply the normalization.

Collect the aggregates and their measurement errors in

$$
\mathbf{g}_{ij}
=
(g_{ikj})_{k\in\mathcal{P}_j}
\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(A)}_{ij}
=
(\epsilon^{(A)}_{ikj})_{k\in\mathcal{P}_j}
\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}.
$$

Let

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{gg,j}
=
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{g}_{ij})
\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{k_j},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{A,j}
=
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(A)}_{ij})
\in\mathbb{S}_+^{k_j}.
$$

The corresponding conditional expectation expression is

$$
E(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}\mid\mathbf{g}_{ij})
=
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}
+
\mathbf{R}_{A,j}
(\mathbf{g}_{ij}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}),
\qquad
\mathbf{R}_{A,j}
=
(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{gg,j}-\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{A,j})
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{gg,j}^{-1}.
$$

As in the scaling version, this is an exact conditional expectation under
joint normality and otherwise a best linear predictor.

Moreover, because the loadings and latent regression slopes are estimated
from centered observations, the empirical aggregates can be calculated
without first estimating intercepts:

$$
\widehat{g}^{\,c}_{ikj}
=
\frac{
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}^{\top}
(\mathbf{y}_{i,kj}-\overline{\mathbf{y}}_{kj})
}{
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}^{\top}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kj}
}.
$$

Let $\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{\,c}_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$ collect these
centered aggregates, and let $\mathbf{S}_{gg,j}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{k_j}$
denote their sample covariance matrix. Under the proxy conditions, the
aggregate error covariance estimate is the diagonal matrix

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{A,j}
=
\operatorname{diag}\left[
\left(
\frac{
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}^{\top}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kj}
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}
}{
\left(
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}^{\top}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kj}
\right)^2
}
\right)_{k\in\mathcal{P}_j}
\right].
$$

The estimated reliability adjustment and centered fitted predictors are

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{A,j}
=
(\mathbf{S}_{gg,j}-c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{A,j})
\mathbf{S}_{gg,j}^{-1},
\qquad
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{\,c,A}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
=
\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{A,j}\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{\,c}_{ij}.
$$

Collecting the fitted predictors in
$\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_j}$ gives

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{j,\mathrm{JSA}}
=
(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A,j}^{\top}
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A,j})^{-1}
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A,j}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_j.
$$

The fitted predictor matrices $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_j$ and
$\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A,j}$ are assumed to have full column rank.

# Estimation of Variance, Covariance, and Intercept Parameters

For each of the three estimators of the factor loadings and latent
regression slopes, the remaining variance and covariance parameters are
estimated by reweighted least squares [@maydeuolivares_etall_2026], holding
these estimates fixed throughout the iterations. Let

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{H}}
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}
(\mathbf{I}_q-\widehat{\mathbf{B}})^{-1}
\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q},
$$
where $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}$ and $\widehat{\mathbf{B}}$ are
obtained using the selected estimator, MIIV, JS, or JSA, assuming that
$\mathbf{I}_q-\widehat{\mathbf{B}}$ is nonsingular. Conditional on these
estimates, the implied covariance matrix is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{v})
=
\widehat{\mathbf{H}}\boldsymbol{\Psi}(\mathbf{v})
\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}
+
\boldsymbol{\Theta}(\mathbf{v}),
$$
where $\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v}$ collects the free variance and
covariance parameters.

With fixed entries and linear equality restrictions incorporated into the
parameterization,

$$
\operatorname{vech}\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{v})\}
=
\widehat{\mathbf{c}}+\widehat{\mathbf{G}}\mathbf{v},
$$
where $t=p(p+1)/2$, $\widehat{\mathbf{c}}\in\mathbb{R}^t$ is the fixed
component under the chosen parameterization, and
$\widehat{\mathbf{G}}\in\mathbb{R}^{t\times d_v}$ maps the free parameters to
the implied covariance moments.

For a weight matrix $\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^t$, the weighted
least squares estimate is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{v}}
=
\left(
\widehat{\mathbf{G}}^{\top}
\widehat{\mathbf{W}}
\widehat{\mathbf{G}}
\right)^{-1}
\widehat{\mathbf{G}}^{\top}
\widehat{\mathbf{W}}
\left\{
\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf{S})-\widehat{\mathbf{c}}
\right\},
$$
assuming that $\widehat{\mathbf{G}}$ has full column rank.

Reweighted least squares updates the normal theory weight matrix
[@browne_1974] using the current implied covariance matrix:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{W}}^{(\tau)}
=
\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{D}_p^{\top}
\left[
\{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(\tau)}\}^{-1}
\otimes
\{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(\tau)}\}^{-1}
\right]\mathbf{D}_p,
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(\tau)}
=
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\widehat{\mathbf{v}}^{(\tau)}).
$$

Here, $\otimes$ denotes the Kronecker product, and
$\mathbf{D}_p\in\mathbb{R}^{p^2\times t}$ is the duplication matrix
satisfying
$\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{S})=\mathbf{D}_p\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf{S})$.
At iteration $\tau$, substituting $\widehat{\mathbf{W}}^{(\tau)}$ into the
weighted least squares expression gives $\widehat{\mathbf{v}}^{(\tau+1)}$. The
updates are repeated until convergence, assuming that the implied
covariance matrices used to construct the weights remain positive definite.
The resulting $\widehat{\mathbf{v}}$ determines $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}$
and $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}$, which are not constrained to be positive
semidefinite.

Finally, the intercepts are estimated from the sample means, using the
previously estimated factor loadings and latent regression slopes.
Under the scaling indicator parameterization, the mean structure is
saturated when all nonscaling indicator intercepts and all structural
intercepts are free. Let $\overline{\mathbf{m}}\in\mathbb{R}^q$ contain the
sample scaling indicator means. Then

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_\eta
=
\overline{\mathbf{m}},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
=
\overline{\mathbf{y}}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}\overline{\mathbf{m}}
\in\mathbb{R}^p,
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
=
(\mathbf{I}_q-\widehat{\mathbf{B}})
\overline{\mathbf{m}}
\in\mathbb{R}^q.
$$

These expressions preserve the fixed zero scaling indicator intercepts and reproduce
the observed sample means. Additional mean structure restrictions require a
corresponding constrained estimation step. Together, these stages estimate the 
free entries of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$,
$\boldsymbol{\Psi}$, $\boldsymbol{\nu}$, and $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$. Although
the estimated factor loadings and latent regression slopes are held fixed
during covariance estimation, their sampling uncertainty is propagated when
calculating standard errors. 

# Analytical Standard Errors

For the MIIV estimates of the factor loadings and latent regression slopes,
the conventional homoskedastic covariance estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{j,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
\widehat{\sigma}_{u_j}^{\,2}
(\mathbf{X}_j^{\top}\mathbf{P}_j\mathbf{X}_j)^{-1}
\in\mathbb{S}_+^{k_j},
$$
where

$$
\widehat{\sigma}_{u_j}^{\,2}
=
\frac{\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_j^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_j}
{n-k_j-1},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_j
=
\mathbf{d}_j-\mathbf{X}_j\widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{j,\mathrm{MIIV}},
$$
where the intercept is absorbed by centering and $n>k_j+1$. Here,
$\sigma_{u_j}^{2}$ is the composite error variance of the L2O equation,
rather than an individual measurement error or structural disturbance
variance.

This equation specific expression concerns the factor loadings and latent
regression slopes. For the variance and covariance parameters
$\mathbf{v}$, the delta method is applied to the second stage. Let
$\widehat{\mathbf{H}}_2=(\widehat{\mathbf{G}}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\widehat{\mathbf{G}})^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{G}}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{W}}$
be evaluated at the converged weights and treated as fixed, as in
@bollen_maydeuolivares_2007 and @jin_etall_2021, let $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_1$
be the Jacobian of $\operatorname{vech}\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\}$
with respect to the factor loadings and latent regression slopes,
evaluated at the estimates, and let $\widehat{\mathbf{K}}$ be the Jacobian
of their MIIV estimates with respect to $\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf{S})$
[@fisher_bollen_2020]. Under correct specification, the estimated
covariance matrix is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{v},\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
\frac{1}{n}
\widehat{\mathbf{H}}_2
(\mathbf{I}_t-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_1\widehat{\mathbf{K}})
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}_{S}
(\mathbf{I}_t-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_1\widehat{\mathbf{K}})^{\top}
\widehat{\mathbf{H}}_2^{\top}
\in\mathbb{S}_+^{d_v},
$$
where $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}_{S}\in\mathbb{S}_+^{t}$ estimates the
asymptotic covariance matrix of $\sqrt{n}\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf{S})$.
The factor $\mathbf{I}_t-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_1\widehat{\mathbf{K}}$
propagates the sampling uncertainty of the estimated factor loadings and
latent regression slopes through the residual moments. The standard errors of the MIIV intercept estimates
follow from the same argument applied to the mean structure step.

@burghgraeve_etall_2021 derived a variance expression for the latent
regression slopes that accounts for the estimated reliability
adjustment and used bootstrap standard errors in their evaluations. Here,
analytical standard errors are obtained by differentiating the complete
estimation procedure with respect to the sample moments. For
$T\in\{\mathrm{JS},\mathrm{JSA}\}$, write

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_T=g_{n,T}(\mathbf{s}),
$$
where $g_{n,T}$ maps the $h$ sample moments to the $d$ parameter estimates.
This mapping includes the preliminary error variance estimates, the
estimates of the factor loadings and latent regression slopes, the
subsequent variance and covariance estimates, and the intercept estimates.

Suppose

$$
\sqrt{n}\{
\mathbf{s}-\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
\}
\xrightarrow{d}
N_h(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Gamma}),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\in\mathbb{S}_+^h,
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is the joint asymptotic covariance matrix of the
sample means and covariances. Under the required moment and
differentiability conditions, the delta method covariance estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_T
=
\frac{1}{n}
\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_T
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}
\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_T^{\top}
\in\mathbb{S}_+^d,
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_T
=
\left.
\frac{\partial g_{n,T}(\mathbf{s})}
{\partial\mathbf{s}^{\top}}
\right|_{\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{obs}}}
\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times h}.
$$

The Jacobian is evaluated analytically by default by differentiating the
estimation steps. For reweighted least squares, the derivative is obtained by implicit
differentiation of the converged estimating equations. The Jacobian
propagates uncertainty through the preliminary error variance estimates,
reliability adjustments, estimates of the factor loadings and latent
regression slopes, variance and covariance estimates, and intercept
estimates. For JSA, it also accounts for the estimated aggregation
weights and normalization loadings.

The matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ can be estimated using normal theory or
empirical moments through order four [@browne_1984]. Normal theory
estimates may be evaluated at the sample covariance matrix or the fitted
model covariance matrix. For parameter
$r=1,\ldots,d$, the analytical standard error is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat{\theta}_{T,r})
=
\sqrt{[\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_T]_{rr}}
\in[0,\infty).
$$

For MIIV factor loadings and latent regression slopes, moment based
covariance estimates are also available as
$n^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{K}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}_S\widehat{\mathbf{K}}^{\top}$.
Together with the second stage expression and the mean structure step
above, these provide delta method standard errors calculated separately
for each parameter block.

# Simulation Design and Performance Evaluation

In this section we describe the design of the simulation study and the
measures used to evaluate the standard errors.

### Population Model and Estimands

We study the model in @fig-model, with three latent variables and four
indicators each. The latent variable model is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{2}&=\alpha_2+B_{21}\eta_{1}+\zeta_{2},\\
\eta_{3}&=\alpha_3+B_{31}\eta_{1}+B_{32}\eta_{2}+\zeta_{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pop-structural}

The design is partly based on previous studies. @burghgraeve_etall_2021
used four indicators per latent variable, a common reliability of .6 or .8
for all indicators. Note also that the model is similar to the empirical 
illustration @burghgraeve_etall_2021. Moreover, 
@jin_etall_2021 used a recursive latent variable model with several equations 
and standardized slopes between 0.1 and 0.6, 
which the present model follows with $B_{21}=0.6$, $B_{31}=0.3$, and
$B_{32}=0.5$. With $\operatorname{Var}(\eta_1)=1$,
$\operatorname{Var}(\zeta_2)=0.64$, and $\operatorname{Var}(\zeta_3)=0.48$,
the variances of $\eta_2$ and $\eta_3$ equal 1, so that the slopes
are standardized, and the implied correlations are .60 between $\eta_1$
and $\eta_2$, .60 between $\eta_1$ and $\eta_3$, and .68 between $\eta_2$
and $\eta_3$. The scaling indicators have loadings fixed to one and the
remaining loadings range from 0.8 to 1.2. The mean structure has
$E(\eta_1)=1$, $\alpha_2=\alpha_3=0.5$, and intercepts of 0.2 for the
nonscaling indicators. The main estimands are all free factor
loadings, latent regression slopes, residual variances, and latent variances
and disturbance variances.

```{tikz}
%| echo: false

\usetikzlibrary{arrows.meta}

    \node[obs] (y\k) at (\x, -4.5) {$y_{\k}$};

    \node[obs] (y\k) at (\x, -4.5) {$y_{\k}$};
  \draw[->] (e1) -- node[lab] {$1$} (y1);
  \draw[->] (e1) -- node[lab] {$\lambda_2$} (y2);
  \draw[->] (e1) -- node[lab] {$\lambda_3$} (y3);

```

### Simulation Conditions and Estimation Approaches

We employed a fully factorial design with two factors: sample size
($n\in\{100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600\}$) and indicator reliability
($\rho\in\{.6, .8\}$). This yielded $6\times2=12$ conditions, each
replicated 1,500 times. The sample sizes cover the small to moderate range
in which the equation by equation estimators are expected to differ most
from maximum likelihood. The reliability levels match the low and high
conditions of @burghgraeve_etall_2021 and determine the size of the
reliability adjustment in the James–Stein estimators.

As highlighted, we investigated the JS, JSA, MIIV-2SLS, and ML approaches, all
with the default options in lavaan. 

### Data Generation

Data were generated from the population model with all stochastic
components normal and mutually independent. The exogenous latent variable
was generated as $\eta_1\sim\mathcal{N}(1,1)$ and the structural
disturbances as $\zeta_2\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.64)$ and
$\zeta_3\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.48)$, from which $\eta_2$ and $\eta_3$ follow
by @eq-pop-structural. The measurement error of each indicator was
generated as normal with mean zero and variance $\lambda^2(1-\rho)/\rho$,
where $\lambda$ is the loading of that indicator, so that every indicator
has reliability $\rho$ in its condition, and the indicators follow by the
measurement equations. The observed variables are therefore multivariate
normal with the mean vector and covariance matrix implied by the
population values. All four estimators were applied to the same data
sets.

### Convergence, Outliers, and Inadmissible Solutions

Replications were screened in two steps, and a replication that failed
either step for any estimator was removed for all four. A solution was
nonconverged when any estimate, standard error, or confidence interval
bound of an estimand was missing or non-finite. Among the converged
replications, outliers were point estimates more than three interquartile
ranges below the first or above the third quartile, per condition,
estimator, and estimand. Inadmissible
solutions, with a nonpositive variance estimate, were retained and
counted.

### Performance Measures

Performance was assessed with the measures implemented in the simhelpers
package [@joshi_pustejovsky_2025], computed for every estimand. These
measures, with their empirical and Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE)
calculations, are listed in @tbl-performance. The MCSEs of the SD and
of the SE$^2$/VAR ratio are obtained by jackknife and that of coverage in
closed form. The SE/SD ratio and the SE$^2$/VAR ratio compare the same
quantities on the standard deviation and on the variance scale, so only
the latter, for which an MCSE is available, is shown in the figures.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Performance Measures for Evaluating the Standard Errors"
#| apa-note: "$\\hat\\theta_k$ is the estimate of parameter $\\theta$ in replication $k$ ($k = 1, \\dots, K$) and $\\bar{\\theta}$ the mean of the $K$ estimates. $\\widehat{SE}_k$ is the estimated standard error in replication $k$, $\\overline{SE} = \\tfrac{1}{K}\\sum_k \\widehat{SE}_k$, $\\overline{SE^2} = \\tfrac{1}{K}\\sum_k \\widehat{SE}_k^2$, and $L_k, U_k$ are the confidence interval limits. The subscript $(j)$ marks a leave-one-out jackknife replicate. The dash marks an MCSE that is not computed."
tab <- data.frame(
  measure = c("SD", "SE/SD ratio", "SE$^2$/VAR ratio", "Coverage"),
  empirical = c("$S_{\\hat\\theta}=\\sqrt{\\tfrac{1}{K-1}\\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\\hat\\theta_k-\\bar{\\theta})^2}$",
                "$\\overline{SE}/S_{\\hat\\theta}$",
                "$\\nu=\\overline{SE^2}/S_{\\hat\\theta}^2$",
                "$c=\\tfrac{1}{K}\\sum_{k=1}^{K}I(L_k\\le\\theta\\le U_k)$"),
  mcse = c("$\\sqrt{\\tfrac{K-1}{K}\\sum_{j=1}^{K}(S_{(j)}-S_{\\hat\\theta})^2}$",
           "---",
           "$\\sqrt{\\tfrac{K-1}{K}\\sum_{j=1}^{K}(\\nu_{(j)}-\\nu)^2}$",
           "$\\sqrt{c(1-c)/K}$"))
knitr::asis_output(paste0("\\begin{center}\n",
  knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, longtable = TRUE,
               linesep = "", format = "latex",
               col.names = c("Performance measure", "Empirical calculation", "MCSE")),
  "\n\\end{center}"))
```

### Reproducibility and Computational Details

All analyses were conducted in R [@rcoreteam_2025] using the lavaan package
[@rosseel_2012] for estimation, simhelpers [@joshi_pustejovsky_2025] for
performance evaluation, and ggplot2 [@wickham_2016] for the figures. The
computational environment was pinned with Nix [@dolstra_etall_2004] via the
rix package [@rodrigues_baumann_2026], and the article was written with the
apaquarto extension [@schneider_2026]. The replication level estimates,
standard errors, and confidence intervals, the performance measures, and
the screening counts are saved as R data files in the project repository,
together with the R version, package versions, code, and manuscript.

```{r}
#| label: performance
source("performance_calculation.R")
library(ggplot2)
summ$class <- ifelse(grepl("=~", summ$parameter), "Loadings",
               ifelse(grepl("~~", summ$parameter),
                      ifelse(grepl("^eta", summ$parameter), "Factor variances",
                             "Residual variances"), "Structural"))
summ$estimator <- factor(summ$estimator,
                         levels = c("JS", "JSA", "IV", "ML"))

## long format over the three criteria, with values above `cap` flagged
crit <- c(sd = "SD", rb_var = "SE²/VAR", coverage = "Coverage")
mcse <- c(sd = "sd_mcse", rb_var = "rb_var_mcse", coverage = "coverage_mcse")
cap <- 1.5
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(crit), function(k)
  data.frame(summ[c("n", "rel", "estimator", "parameter", "class")],
             criterion = crit[k],
             value = summ[[k]],
             mcse = summ[[mcse[k]]])))
long$criterion <- factor(long$criterion, levels = crit)
ref <- data.frame(criterion = factor(c("SE²/VAR", "Coverage"), levels = crit),
                  y = c(1, 0.95))
clip <- function(v) {
  i <- v$criterion == "SE²/VAR"
  v$clipped <- i & v$value > cap
  v$value[v$clipped] <- cap
  if ("upper" %in% names(v)) {
    v$upper[i] <- pmin(v$upper[i], cap)
    v$lower[i] <- pmin(v$lower[i], cap)
    v$lower[v$clipped] <- v$upper[v$clipped] <- NA
  }
  v
}
pd <- position_dodge(width = 25)
plot_perf <- function(v, col, labeller = "label_value", breaks = ns) {
  ggplot(v, aes(n, value, colour = estimator, shape = estimator,
                linetype = estimator)) +
    geom_hline(data = ref, aes(yintercept = y), colour = "grey55",
               linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0,
                  linetype = "solid", position = pd, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, position = pd) +
    geom_point(size = 2, position = pd) +
    geom_point(data = v[v$clipped, ], shape = 2, size = 3, position = pd,
               show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_grid(as.formula(paste("rel + criterion ~", col)),
               scales = "free_y", switch = "y", labeller = labeller) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = breaks) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(JS = "#2a78d6", JSA = "#eda100",
                                   IV = "#eb6834", ML = "#1baf7a")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(JS = 16, JSA = 18, IV = 15, ML = 17)) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(JS = "solid", JSA = "dashed",
                                     IV = "longdash", ML = "dotdash")) +
    labs(x = expression(italic(n)), y = NULL, colour = "Estimator",
         shape = "Estimator", linetype = "Estimator") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.placement = "outside",
          strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 90),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "grey80"))
}
plot_params <- function(pars, labels, breaks = ns) {
  v <- long[long$parameter %in% pars, ]
  v$parameter <- factor(v$parameter, levels = pars, labels = labels)
  v$rel <- factor(v$rel, levels = rels,
                  labels = paste("Reliability", sub("^0", "", rels)))
  v$lower <- v$value - v$mcse; v$upper <- v$value + v$mcse
  plot_perf(clip(v), "parameter",
            labeller = labeller(parameter = label_parsed), breaks = breaks)
}
pars_coef <- c("eta2~eta1", "eta3~eta1", "eta3~eta2")
lab_coef  <- c("B[21]", "B[31]", "B[32]")
pars_load <- c("eta1=~y2", "eta2=~y6", "eta3=~y10")
lab_load  <- c("lambda[2]", "lambda[6]", "lambda[10]")
pars_res  <- c("y1~~y1", "y2~~y2", "y5~~y5", "y6~~y6", "y9~~y9", "y10~~y10")
lab_res   <- c("theta[1]", "theta[2]", "theta[5]", "theta[6]", "theta[9]",
               "theta[10]")
pars_fvar <- c("eta1~~eta1", "eta2~~eta2", "eta3~~eta3")
lab_fvar  <- c("Var(eta[1])", "Var(zeta[2])", "Var(zeta[3])")
```

# Results

## Convergence, Outliers, and Inadmissible Solutions

All four estimators converged in every replication of every condition.
Outlier screening removed `r scr$removed` of the 18,000 replications
(`r sprintf("%.2f", scr$removed_pct)`%), concentrated at $n=100$ with
reliability .6, where `r sprintf("%.1f", scr$removed_by_cond[1])`% of the
replications were removed, flagged mainly through JS
(`r sprintf("%.1f", scr$flagged_100_06["JS"])`% of the replications in that
condition). In every other condition fewer than 0.5% of the replications were
removed. Inadmissible solutions occurred in `r scr$inad` replications, all
for JS at $n=100$ with reliability .6, where a residual or disturbance
variance estimate was nonpositive. They are included in the results
below.

## Standard Error Performance

Each figure shows reliability .6 in the upper half and reliability .8 in
the lower half. @fig-sim-structural shows the latent regression slopes,
@fig-sim-loadings one factor loading per latent variable,
@fig-sim-residual the residual variances of the scaling indicators and of
one nonscaling indicator per latent variable, and @fig-sim-factorvar the
variance of $\eta_1$ and the two disturbance variances. The loadings and
residual variances not shown behave like those shown for the same latent
variable, with SE$^2$/VAR ratios within 0.14 and coverage within .03 of
each other in every condition.

From $n=300$ onward, the four estimators are indistinguishable within
Monte Carlo error. The SE$^2$/VAR ratio stays within 0.11 of one and
coverage within .035 of .95 for every estimator and parameter at both
reliability levels, and the curves move together across sample sizes
because they are computed on the same data sets. Three differences appear
at $n=100$ and $n=200$, mainly at reliability .6.

First, the scaling James–Stein standard errors for the slopes $B_{31}$
and $B_{32}$ are too large at reliability .6, with SE$^2$/VAR ratios of
1.5 to 1.6 at $n=100$ and 1.13 at $n=200$ and coverage of .96 to .98,
while the SD is also the largest of the four, 0.24 against 0.13 to 0.17
at $n=100$. In some replications the reliability adjustment for the
equation of $\eta_3$ implies a correlation between $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$
close to one, so that the fitted predictors are nearly collinear and both
the estimates and their standard errors are inflated. The screening
removed the most extreme of these replications, the milder ones remain.
The aggregated estimator, which pools all indicators of a latent
variable, is unaffected.

Second, the MIIV loadings undercover at reliability .6, with coverage of
.88 to .89 at $n=100$ against .93 to .95 for the other estimators, while
the MIIV SE$^2$/VAR ratio is 1.05 to 1.07 and its SD the smallest. The
gap comes from a downward bias of about 0.06 in the two-stage least
squares loadings when the scaling indicators are unreliable, a weak
instrument effect also reported by @jin_etall_2021, and it fades slowly
with sample size.

Third, the disturbance variances separate the estimators at $n=100$. ML
undercovers them, at .91 to .94, although its SE$^2$/VAR ratio is close
to one, MIIV overcovers them, at .96 to .97, with ratios of 1.11 to 1.18,
and the James–Stein estimators lie in between. At reliability .8 the
disturbance variance of $\eta_2$ is undercovered at .92 by ML and by both
James–Stein estimators alike. The residual variances show no such
contrast, with coverage between .92 and .96 for all estimators and a
common dip at $n=100$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-structural
#| fig-cap: "Performance of the Standard Errors of the Latent Regression Slopes"
#| apa-note: "NoNote *Note.* JS = scaling James–Stein, JSA = aggregated James–Stein, IV = MIIV-2SLS, ML = maximum likelihood. Dotted lines mark the reference values 1 and .95. Error bars represent Monte Carlo standard errors. Values above 1.5 are drawn at 1.5 with an open triangle."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| out-width: "100%"
plot_params(pars_coef, lab_coef)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-loadings

#| apa-note: "NoNote *Note.* JS = scaling James–Stein, JSA = aggregated James–Stein, IV = MIIV-2SLS, ML = maximum likelihood. Dotted lines mark the reference values 1 and .95. Error bars represent Monte Carlo standard errors. Values above 1.5 are drawn at 1.5 with an open triangle."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| out-width: "100%"
plot_params(pars_load, lab_load)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
```
